utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. A very good afternoon to everybody. May we hear the case in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask how many witnesses will be here for this week. You have concrete knowledge now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have available three witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We plan that the second witness might take two days, depending on the cross-examination and the questions of Your Honours, so -- we think that we have covered four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Four days. So let's wait and see, and we have to come back to this question of witnesses immediately. I just have to inform you that ten minutes ago I learned that there was another -- there will be another extraordinary bureau meeting held on Wednesday at 2.00. Would there be any problem for the parties, in case we would have to switch from morning to exchange with Judge Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No problem. We are even ready not to work that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't share the latter part of your view. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have no problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I will inform you as soon as possible what will be possible in the next week. Let me take the opportunity to address some open questions, because when there are problems, they could be discussed immediately, not put under the carpet in -- also in order that the parties know how the proceedings will continue. And therefore, the first question would be for the Defence. I already asked the question on how can we manage to hear 34 witnesses and two additional experts when at the same time we have only 33 days available? Is -- did you already take into account to 92 bis the one or another witness -- did you take into account to take -- to request for taking depositions in order to avoid problems with witnesses not prepared to come to The Hague but, on the other hand, prepared to testify or make use of the possibility of a videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For now, we know that two of our witnesses will ask for the videolink. One cannot fly. And another one has some sick member of family and he cannot abandon that member. So for two of them, we know that there would -- there would be a videolink. And regarding 92 bis, we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Step by step. May I ask, did you already discuss this with the Registry? Because I know that establishing such a videolink takes time, human resources, and we need to know this in advance. I think, Madam Registrar, correct me if I'm wrong, a minimum of three to four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We haven't discussed it yet, Your Honour. We will probably discuss it today or tomorrow at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I should appreciate it. 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are reviewing our witnesses, and obviously we will have to have some 92 bis witnesses instead of having them live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are looking for which -- for the motion. It might be a relative -- a short one, and only that we know what is the basis and -- and may it be discussed amongst the parties before a motion be filed that when there are obstacles from the point of view of the Prosecution, then maybe it's unnecessary to file a motion. If the OTP immediately agree, then it can be a very short motion. I know about your personal workload, Mr. Lukic. What about depositions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Depositions -- we'll know about depositions in three weeks. So today I cannot really tell anything about depositions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You should take into account that it would be an advantage and it would limit the costs if the depositions could be taken at the same time we have the videolink from -- from wheresoever in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So therefore, please be aware of the link of this problem, depositions to be taken and videolink. Then it might be helpful to address it, this question at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We had -- or better said, in this case - I didn't discuss this problem previously with my colleagues - but when revisiting the transcripts of the last two weeks, I had the problem -- the impression that there were the following problems: First, how to cure the late disclosure. And it transpires from transcript page 10.616, that -- not to repeat the same words that the Defence was not amused at all that the OTP has had the opportunity to open their case, to ask questions, to submit new evidence, and to continue to establish their case. And it transpires that, therefore, you would not be asking Dr. Mujadzic and then later on Mr. Mayhew any other questions. Therefore, it should be clarified, the way how to cure these problems emanating from the apparent late disclosure of six statements. First, as a matter of principle and following the rules of logic, it is only possible to hear once again and to re-cross-examine or additional cross-examine a witness when the case of the Prosecutor is reopened. There can't be a cross-examination of a OTP witness within the Defence case. That's also a question of balancing the time. But this is not the predominant question. The predominant question is that in fact there was a possibility to ask questions, to submit new evidence, because here the scenario was different to the scenario related to five other statements. In the case we had before us - and I refer to the line of questions prepared in writing by the Defence - the new questions were emanating from the statement disclosed -- late disclosed but disclosed in August, the statement of Mr. Srdjo Srdic. And there was, therefore, in practice no prejudice at all because Witness Sivac had already been heard at that point in time. Here the intention was to give at the same time the possibility of re-cross-examination but also to avoid that during rebuttal, during rejoinder, or proprio motu by the Appeals Chamber Witness Sivac would have to come another to this Tribunal, and therefore the opportunity was taken to hear him immediately. In case the line of questions to be put on the basis of an additional cross-examination to a witness - and this would be based on one of the five other statements - no doubt we would immediately start after having, as mentioned, reopened the Prosecution's case, with the cross-examination. But there is no impediment at all and there is no possibility to stop the Prosecution to re-examine as usual or the Judges to put additional questions to the witness when called a second time for the purpose of re-cross-examination. So therefore, this distinction has to be drawn only in this -- if the request is based on questions emanating from the five statements taken before the beginning of this case and which should have been available for both the Defence and the Judges, then it is -- if all the other prerequisites are met, to reproduce the status quo ante. I hope that in this connection there are no further misunderstandings that would lead the Defence not to request a re-cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we said, the aim of the whole proceeding with calling witnesses back is to cure something that was missed on the Prosecution side. There is nothing to be cured. They had the statements. They knew about the facts. They could have asked anything those witnesses immediately. So there is nothing to be cured on their side. Their questions were put without the Defence having those questions in writing, as was ordered to the Defence. The Defence had to submit the questions in writing, and the Prosecution didn't have to do the same thing. I don't know why that distinction was made. So we think that if the Prosecution evidence cannot be given during the Defence case giving the right to the Prosecution to cross-examine the same witnesses again, then we can agree that only the Defence has the right to cure the damage that has been done to the Defence. So I would agree if somebody can establish that there is any kind of damage done to the Defence with their late disclosure of these statements. And that's why -- exactly why the Defence does not want these witnesses back to allow the Prosecution to have their case in chief during the Defence case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before giving the floor to the Prosecution, I have to re-emphasise the distinction has to be made between those five statements that were available from the beginning of this case. There it's quite clear. And we requested the line of questions only that we knew whether or not there could have been a prejudice emanating from the fact of this late disclosure, and on this basis we could decide whether it would be for us to re-call -- or request the Prosecution to re-call this witness. This was not the case with the six statements -- sixth statement not available when we heard Mr. Sivac. So this first threshold is to show good cause to hear the witness once again. Then it can be cured by opening -- reopening the cross-examination. But at the same time, the same rules apply, what happens after a cross-examination. On the same scope, what will be covered by the Defence, it is for the OTP to right to re-examine and for the Judges in the same area covering the same terrain to put questions to the witness when a witness comes back. If we are in this second category emanating from the five statements, the Trial Chamber will not allow to add new evidence because this would be then later during the period of rebuttal, but not now. It was due to the distinction we had to make and the basis of what you have shown when you requested the re-cross-examination of this witness. In this case, it was different, and therefore in order -- as stated to avoid a third appearance of this person, we proceeded as foreseen, but I think you will understand this distinction. But now, please for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to repeat what the Court has already said. I would just point out that as to Mr. Sivac, the questions that were written by the Defence all dealt with areas outside of the five statements that were taken before Mr. Sivac testified. None of them had to do with those five interviews which the Prosecution disclosed after Mr. Sivac testified. The questions had to do with the sixth interview that occurred after his testimony and with other evidence that the Defence obtained subsequent to him testifying. The Prosecution questions dealt with matters learned while he was here on the Brdjanin case, but I think all -- if not all, almost all the questions dealt with the newspaper articles which were mentioned in his court examination the first time he testified. He indicated he had these articles and the Court asked him to provide those to the Prosecution because we did a videolink the rest of the day, that was never presented. So it was, in a way, reopening that portion that was left open the last time he was here because we didn't have time for him to retrieve those newspaper articles and to bring them to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope it's clear now for the Defence how the Court will proceed in future in case there is a request. The question depends on what the line of questions are based. And of course, the purpose of requesting the line of questions is not to ask you for a -- the entire line of questions, if only on the basis of one question it is shown that the threshold is met, that we can reopen the cross-examination. And when it's based on the five late testimony only, we will start with the re-cross-examination immediately. Then another area: It was only last Friday the Defence complained about the facts that previous statements or parts of the transcript were put to a witness, and it was submitted this would not be in line with previous rulings in this case. Having revisited the former transcripts, I think it's absolutely clear that it is possible for both parties and for the Judges to confront the witnesses with all kinds of admitted evidence, be it video, be it an exhibit, or be it a former testimony from our transcript. What was demanded in the past and will be demanded in the future remains the same, to quote correctly without any omissions and in context and adding the page of transcript that everybody can control, whether this was the adequate quotation, and later on when we have to evaluate the evidence, that it facilitates the search for this previous testimony. So there's nothing special to put a former statement given by a witness to another witness. It was only the question of the language that I asked the Defence to rephrase a question because it would not be correct, say -- now it's not from any transcript. It's just to give you an example. It would not be correct to quote if another witness would have stated, Would you call him a liar? This is not appropriate, both because it's not the correct way to put the question to the witness or the former testimony to the witness, and it's not the adequate way. It's just serving for the purposes of refreshing the memory of the witness and to confront the witness and maybe this is, in fact, in addition of assistance or an attempt coming closer to the truth. And we would appreciate that always in cases that there is a clear discrepancy between witness statements that already and during the cross-examination by the Office of the Prosecutor these discrepancies would be highlighted and in this way clarified, because for the Judges it's absolutely impossible knowingly to omit to put questions to a witness when we have a clear discrepancy of two witness statements. And therefore, we have to find out, and one way of how to find out the best possible way and how to come as close as possible to truth is to confront a witness with a previous statement given here in the formal form of evidence. A second point, no doubt, is statements. And also here in the past the ruling was that it would be only not allowed to ask out of the blue if any witness would say the following: How would you comment on this? Good cause must be shown and it must be shown that there is an underlying basis for this question. For example, a previous statement given in a formal setting to the OTP made available under 65 ter or under 68 or other Rules, but there must be a sound basis for this question. And if so, no doubt also this in the appropriate way and in the appropriate language can be put to the witness. And this is not only reflected in the rulings as such -- I would have a number of examples available -- but the -- I want to make reference to the minutes dated 23 January 2003. And for the purposes of this small section, this strict confidentiality is lifted. I quote from this. Here it states -- Ms. Korner objects to the form of question: "What would you say if you knew what Srdic said," which she considers improper. And then it continues, "Judge Schomburg disagrees and states that it's a right of the Defence to ask this question and of" -- "from the minutes." So there can't be any doubt what the position of the Judges of this Trial Chamber related to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can state here that I'm 100 per cent sure that this right was denied to the Defence during the Prosecution case. I will use it very often if I were allowed to do it. Now this is introduced to this case when we cannot use this rule any more. We don't have Prosecution witnesses any more. If this is a ruling of this Chamber, we would like the certificate to appeal this ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If this is -- as I emphasised in the beginning, it's not a ruling of the Chamber; it's only an explanation and a compilation of that what can be found on the transcripts and what can be found in the minutes. And maybe you recall, this was already in April or was it the first week of May discussed in the framework of a meeting on the question of leading and misleading questions. And there it was held that a question would be misleading if there wouldn't be a sound basis, be it on a former transcript or a former statement. But there was no obstacle at all, and this was emphasised already in April and May 2002 that there's no obstacle at all to put this to witness only if there is a sound basis for putting these questions or previous statements to the witness. It is only a compilation. It's no ruling. It's a summary of that what has been said in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what the Defence had right is to present to the witness his own previous statements. We were never allowed to present the witness anybody else's statement, never during the case, never. We cannot have -- have a case, the Prosecution case without this right when the Defence should have used it and then have the Defence case with this right for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think my statement was quite clear that the same ruling was already made in April/May 2002. It's only a summary. May I hear submissions by the Prosecution if they so want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have any submissions because I think we're -- with all due respect to counsel and the Court, it's so general right now that we're not accomplishing much by talking about it, what happened months ago, unless we could point to specific instances. So I think the record speaks for itself. We're confident that the record is complete and supports that both sides have had a right to a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Another point is that we -- the Judges and first of all the Defence apparently were taken by surprise to be confronted with three additional documents which not were presented under Rule 65 ter and which in fact tend to be of relevance for this case. The Defence indicated that they would move on this issue. Could you please explain your complaints on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would ask kindly the permission of Your Honours to postpone this until tomorrow, because Mr. Ostojic is in charge of this part, so I'm really not following this closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe a submission that may be of assistance by the Prosecution why this late disclosure of these three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't present in court, but I would say as a general rule where required by Rule 65 ter to provide all the documents we intend to use, obviously at the time we begin our case. During the Defence case, some points became relevant that we were not aware of because we don't know what the Defence is going to put on until they present that evidence. When they do present that evidence, we do not believe that the Rules require us or preclude us from producing additional document that may now become relevant and that we now intend to use but did not intend to use earlier. We think the Rules only require us to disclose Rule 68 documents pre-trial at the time and those documents we intend to use. But obviously during the Defence case we may -- documents may become relevant that we did not anticipate as being relevant earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think based on this we may hear the comments by Mr. Ostojic tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this is now in both directions, in the direction of both parties. There were serious complaints on the application and implementation of Rule 91 during the case. I recall the strong complaint by Ms. Korner following the testimony of a British witness, and last week we heard in return some similar complaints by the Defence. Therefore, also here it seems to be necessary to give some general remarks. Unfortunately, Rule 91(A) does not give any guideline when to warn a witness of the duty to tell the truth. Unfortunately, because in numerous legal systems it is the duty for the Judges to inform a witness on the consequences that may result from a failure to tell the truth. In the beginning of a witness statement related to each and every witness, I don't know why in Rule 91 it reads only "may," and it's not mandatory, because normally also a witness should be informed on the consequences. The Defence took the liberty to try to make the statement that based on this application of Rule 91, witnesses would not come to The Hague. I think one should take care that this doesn't become a self-fulfilling prophesy when stating that a witness would not be treated in all the necessary fairness in this Tribunal. And as to the fact that we heard the complaints also from the Prosecution, it should be quite clear that we have only the interest to hear witnesses stating the truth and nothing but the truth, and there should no approach be taken in that way that from the outset a witness from the other side should be regarded as a liar. I don't want to repeat this from transcripts in order to avoid -- to worsen the situation, but it is no doubt the obligation to take care that a witness tells us the truth. And when a witness changes the testimony within minutes, it's no doubt reason enough to give this warning. And what has been said, especially by the last witness, is a good example that the witness does not regard this as an obstacle to testify but really to concentrate and to provide us with that what taking into account the long period of time since 1992 he or she believes is the truth. We take into account that the recollection may change, that it might be misleading, that a person might try to forget, might try only in order to survive -- to forget about all these heinous crimes and, therefore, is in fact without lying not able to tell us what happened at that time any longer. We are aware of this. And we are also aware of the fact that it's difficult, no doubt for different reasons, for both parties to bring witnesses to The Hague. But we can only be interested in witnesses trying to tell us the truth. Otherwise, other witnesses to hear, we are not interested in. But the presumption should prevail that in principle a witness when appearing tries to tell the truth. I thought one consequence could be that the witness does not have the impression that it's specifically targeted against him or her or to a certain group of witnesses, that it could be possible - because it only reads "may" - that it could be possible to give this admonition or the information of the consequences in all cases in the beginning of the statement. But here I would agree that's too late. We didn't apply this standard from the beginning, and therefore we have to decide also in the future on the case-by-case basis giving, if necessary, the admonition under Rule 91. But please may I ask both parties, refrain from giving the impression that "their" witnesses would be treated different and this would then cause an obstacle for other persons to come here. Everybody -- every witness is welcome, a witness that wants to tell us the truth. Any comments by --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First on this, in my system it's also common that the witnesses warrant what can happen if he lies at the beginning. If it's done in the middle of his testimony, then of course that we cannot expect that the witness continues his testimony in the same manner, not to be frightened and not to feel intimidated. Because it's not my words. That's what I heard from my witnesses and that's what they put in the questionnaires they were given by the Victims and Witnesses Unit, that they were intimidated. It's not my word. That's what I heard from them. That's one point. The second point, when we spoke about the review whether the other party can present the questions of another witness to the present witness. On the page 2.995, during the testimony of Mr. Kapetanovic, line 1, I said -- line 2, I said: "We are not allowed to compare the statements of the witnesses, Your Honour." Then you replied, "Probably you can rephrase your question." We were not allowed during the Prosecution case to compare the statements of different witnesses, only to compare the statements of the same witness. And we stick with this statement. So we would not like to have our witnesses to be subject to something we did not have right to subject the Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think your quotation speaks for itself. May we turn to Rule 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We agree that you can warn the witness before the testimony but not every time when you think that it's different from what the Prosecution witnesses said, because our witnesses really feel it as intimidation. They are frightened. Some of them were in the same area or even this area during this period, and it's very hard to convince them to come here. It's very hard for us. We conducted at least 2.000 interviews. At the end we had 90 witnesses. Now we have in total more than 50. But we will not have them as well if the same rumours were spread in that area. The papers, TV, radio is spreading only sensational news; they don't speak about substance. They speak every time that you warned our witness, that somebody from the Defence side will be punished because that witness lied. And the rest read it, and they don't want to be intimidated. Nobody told me that he does not want or she does not want to come because she's afraid that she or he could be punished. But they have a feeling that they were not treated equally and fairly, as the Prosecution witnesses were treated. So that's what I heard from them. It's not my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But then I think it's for all the parties to inform the witnesses correctly and not to make statements indicating that in the past none of the Prosecution witnesses had been warned in the same way and to make a statement that some of their witnesses, OTP witnesses, they showed 20 times that they lied. Because this is a self-fulfilling prophesy. If you make this statement in the courtroom, then no doubt this will be spread around, and you know yourself well enough that this is not true. And I hope that you revisited transcript page 11.068, where the problem was not the one you mentioned later on page 11.069, making reference to page 88, line 19, that it was a mere fact that the witness within only three minutes gave totally different testimony, and this is, no doubt, reason enough to warn the witness. I think you can agree with this. And therefore, I only wanted to make this once again, because I believe both parties should take care that their statements should not become as such the basis for rumours and the basis for impressions to witnesses that they would be treated in an unfair way. Because I think the witnesses themselves, they have a better sensitivity on this issue and they know from all legal systems of the world that when called as a witness, they have to tell us the truth and nothing but the truth. I think in this -- this exercise to find the truth, it's to the contrary extremely difficult to implement Rule 91 because we have no possibilities at hand to react when we really find out -- to react immediately when we find out that a witness did not answer correctly and in line with the truth and did not as, for example, the witness did in favour of both parties the second day correct in part the previous testimony, and this is the reason why to give such a warning. And if the result is that, as I said, in favour of both parties the witness corrects the statements, then it's just fulfilling the purposes of Rule 91. And therefore, we can be satisfied with the outcome, for example, of the testimony of our last witness, and the same was true also in the past during the Prosecution's case. I recall very well when I cautioned three times one witness, and the outcome at that time was the same positive one. So we have to apply Rule 91. And when it states "may," we have always to exercise our discretion and if necessary we will do so, taking into account that we have to show, as opposed to national legal systems, some self-restraint on the basis of the reasons you have given and the Prosecution has given in the past. So therefore, this explanation how to proceed with Rule 91. Any comments on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just can hope that my witnesses would not give you any grounds to warn them in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then finally please don't misunderstand this, but it seems to be necessary once again to remind the parties that they always have the right - maybe sometimes even the obligation - to object to a form of a question or to a question as such, but please do it in the correct way by standing up. And whenever one is on his or her feet, I will immediately take the first possible opportunity to interrupt to grant the possibility to object. But please refrain from interrupting without having the floor because this could have a detrimental impact on the testimony of a witness, and therefore it's only a question of courtesy to wait until the floor has been given to one of the parties. And please always correct me if I'm wrong, if I have overseen that the one or other party stood up previously. I will always follow the order who stands up first has the first right to take the floor. Any comments on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will try to follow this warnings and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not a warning. It's just a clarification that in the future as a kind of courtesy also vis-a-vis the witnesses they are not interrupted. Thank you. Anything else to be addressed as general problems? At the moment I am aware we still have to come back to the three documents. But anything else beside this? I can't see no requests. Then as usual, the question emanating from your preparation with the witness. Protective measures requested?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures for this witness today. He had protective measures in the past, but I asked him for today. He said I don't need it any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This causes a slight problem. What about the former transcripts and the protective measures there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You may ask maybe him, Your Honour. Maybe he can waive his right to have these transcripts protected. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the OTP would agree to proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that either, whether we're going to need that transcript or to need to refer to it. But I believe both parties have it, so we can proceed -- yes, we agree to proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you -- if you could be so kind and indicate whenever you need to make reference to this previous transcript that we then go into private session and discuss this question with the witness. And in case the witness agrees, then we need not ask, under the Rules, the previous Trial Chamber. I think we should be as flexible and as liberal as possible with this. Yes. No further comments on this specific rule. I think -- may I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dragojevic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. As you know, you are called as a Defence witness. Therefore, the floor is for Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Dragojevic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: My last name is Dragojevic. My first name is Goran. I was born on 18 April 1957 in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you reside currently?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I currently reside in Prijedor in Zmaj Jovan Jovanovica Street, number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your profession, Mr. Dragojevic, in 1992? What did you do in the spring of that year?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I drove an ambulance, and I worked in the Prijedor general hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you start working as an ambulance driver?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I started working as an ambulance driver from 1980 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something about the events prior to April 1992. In 1991 and 1992, did people leave Prijedor municipality? Did they start leaving?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you know about that? How much do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: People started leaving the municipality. They would gather in front of the Patrija department store and the Balkan Hotel. From there they would leave by buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who were the passengers on those buses? What was their age? What was their gender, their ethnicity? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, people who left from in front of the Patrija were mostly Muslims. They were mostly elderly people and women with children. They could easily be recognised by their clothes. The women wore special skirts looking like pants, and the elderly people wore very typical hats on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of that hat?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that a French style hat?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fez, a French style fez hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1991, were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I took my ambulance to Slavonija as driver. So the answer is yes. But soon after that I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you then demobilised?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some one or two months later I was demobilised, and I went back to do the same job that I did before I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you return to? Where did you go back to work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I went back to the medical centre, the Prijedor general hospital, where I worked as an ambulance driver, just like I did before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Up to the end of May 1992, were you mobilised again?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So throughout all that time you worked as a civilian driver of a civilian ambulance.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 30th of April, 1992 there was a takeover in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I am a citizen of Prijedor, and obviously I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the takeover, how did the situation differ as regards the previous days? Was there any change at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The situation didn't change significantly. The only thing that was different was the degree of tension. There was a lot more tension in the air, and one could feel it. People were more tense than they were before that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a killing immediately after the takeover, a killing that you would be aware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime later, since my job was of that nature and I was often in the situation to see what was happening and I could see the wounded. I had to take them to the hospital -- I heard that a young man had been wounded in Prijedor across the road from Bijelo Dugme by the flyover. And there were rumours in the town that the lad had been wounded -- basically not wounded but killed -- by the son of Miralem Ceric who after that escaped and the police were look for him but couldn't find him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the deceased?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: His name was Dzapa Prodin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the suit that he was wearing when he was killed, the clothes that he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what clothes he was wearing at the time, but I heard that he was a member of the reserve police, and I heard it from other people that that's what he was wearing when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the killer's name as well. What is the ethnicity of the person who killed the late Dzapa?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. He lived in Urije.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the existence of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor municipality, and how were you informed about the existence of that body?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of the existence of the Crisis Staff, and I was informed about its existence in the following way: Ambulance drivers had to before filling our tanks with petrol, we had to go to the Crisis Staff and we had to obtain a certificate on which it read how much petrol we were allowed to put into our vehicles at the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where would you go to obtain those certificates, and who was it who issued them to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: We went to the Crisis Staff in Cirkin Polje. There was a house there. And as far as I can remember - it was a long time ago, mind you - there was Mr. Kuruzovic there and his staff were in charge of issuing the certificates. I don't know their names, I'm afraid. We would then use these certificates to go to the petrol station for petrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when was it that you had to go to the Crisis Staff for the first time to obtain your first certificate? In the month of May, when was it exactly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was in late May, before I was wounded. Around the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fighting that took place around Kozarac in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you become familiar with those events, and what was your role as an ambulance driver around those days?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As I was an ambulance driver, our task was one day to go to Susici, a village before Kozarac. It was my colleague and I who went there with an ambulance car, and from there we transported elderly people and children. That was our task, and we were said -- we were told to do that if there was a need to transport the elderly and children. When I got up there, I transported from there in five or six rounds altogether from Susici to town or from Susici to the hospital. I remember very well that I transported Mr. Revko Kapetanovic, him, his old mother, and his wife. I took them to the hospital and then from the hospital I took him to his brother-in-law in Pecani. Mr. Kapetanovic worked in the hospital, in the hospital administration. He was the head accountant in the hospital. I don't know any other persons by name, but I know that there were quite a few of them who were elderly and that there were a few children. I took those people to town and left them either with their relatives or I would leave them in front of the youth centre hall, the so-called Mladost.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it who told you that your last point of call was Susici and that you couldn't go any further with your ambulance?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: When we got up there, the army was already there and they wouldn't let us through, or at least they didn't let the ambulance through. They told us that it was not safe for us to proceed, that we were supposed to pull over and await further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it destroy your line of questioning if we would ask the witness to point out the concrete area?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to put on the ELMO -- sorry, I can't see the exhibit number, but Madam Registrar no doubt has it immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit S14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S14. If you could please be so kind and show us. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. If you could please continue guiding the witness, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please try to point on this map -- could you please face the map. Try to show us the exact location of Susici.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This spot here --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which direction is Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: To the right. To the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So on that day you could only go as far as Susici from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, only this far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to be quite clear, because I can't see Susici on the map, it's between Kozarusa and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you actually read the name "Susici" on the map or you just know where it is, so you're pointing to that spot?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a driver by profession and I drove by Susici plenty of times. It's a village between Kozarusa and Kozarac. Perhaps between 3 and 4 kilometres from the petrol station at the crossroads in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So heading from Prijedor, that's -- Susici is before you reach the petrol station in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That may be between -- around 3 kilometres, between Susici and the petrol station itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be an appropriate time now, Your Honour, for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You pointed out Susici on the map, as we have seen, and that's where you went the day people were leaving Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One day before the conflict in Kozarac, did you drive a patient to Kozarac, which route did you take, and why?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only the day before but also several days before the fighting broke out. But I remember clearly that one day before the fighting in Kozarac erupted, I was driving a pregnant woman and I took her to the centre of Kozarac near the mosque. I left her there, and she went home. A paramedic was accompanying me. If I should state his name -- do you want me to give you his name, the name of the paramedic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, if that's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't see why there should be any problem. The paramedic's name was Irfan Kurtovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you finish with your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This may have escaped you, but I asked you about the route you took to get to Kozarac and why.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I drove down the same route you take to go to Banja Luka, and at the crossroads near the petrol station I turned off the road into the centre of Kozarac and continued for Mrakovica as far as the mosque. The mosque was on the left-hand side just before you leave Kozarac. That's where the pregnant woman got off. Before we arrived there, we were pulled over in two different places; first just next to the sawmill. We were stopped -- we were pulled over by a patrol. The people -- these people were armed, and this man, the paramedic who was with me, he told me there was nothing for me to fear, because those were only guards. They stopped us and inquired about our cargo. When I showed them that there was only the pregnant woman in the ambulance, they allowed us to continue our journey. When we reached the centre of Kozarac, we were again stopped by a patrol, a group consisting of several people, and they asked the same question and I gave them the same answer, and they said it was okay for us to continue. The patient left the car there. I turned the vehicle around and drove back to the Prijedor hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the fighting in Kozarac, there is the attack on Prijedor. Where were you in the morning of the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This morning I was at the hospital. I was on my regular duty, working as an ambulance driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you receive a call on that morning and what were you told?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That morning I received a call at twenty to 5.00. They called me and told me that there was an urgent intervention to be made, an urgent call. So I put on my clothes, because I was in my own room there, the room I was using at the hospital -- I put on my clothes quickly and they told me I should go to the Prijedor Hotel. They said there were patients waiting there to be taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What type of vehicle were you driving at that time as an ambulance driver?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was driving a Lada caravan vehicle. It was an ambulance with very conspicuous red cross insignia. Myself, I was wearing a white overcoat, and I carried also a very visible conspicuous red cross sign on my left arm. That was common for ambulance drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you received this request to go and pick up the patient or patients, did anyone tell you what the ethnic background of those patients were or who you'd be driving, or were you simply told that you would be picking up a patient?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No one informed us of their ethnic background nor of the type of injuries that they had sustained. This is not very common, and as a health worker you would know that they don't tell you this, because all patients were equal for us. I didn't know who I was supposed to be picking up nor what their nationality was. For me it never mattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What time of day was it? Was there light, morning light, or was it still dark?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was called at twenty to 5.00, early in the morning, and I took about five or ten minutes to get ready and start off. It had already dawned and visibility was quite good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened on the way there, as you were on your way to pick up these patients or patient?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Something terrible happened, perhaps one of the most terrible thing that is have ever happened to me in my life. I wouldn't like to see this happen to anyone else ever again. On my way down from the hospital towards the hotel, I was supposed to drive straight under the flyover in order to reach my destination, the destination I was told to go to. Driving towards the flyover at one point I noticed a group of people. There must have been between 14 and 16 people in that group. They were crossing the street. I drove on, not suspecting anything. When I drove up very close to that group, I saw that those people were armed. There were persons I knew in that group, persons I knew from before, from the earlier times. Unsuspecting, I just drove on. The very moment I drove past them -- I drove past them by perhaps half a metre with the front of my car. I missed them by half a metre, and I heard sounds of shooting, firearms being used, a barrage of fire. I still remember the sound of the machine-gun, and I felt sudden pain in my right arm, in my right leg, in my left leg, and my stomach. I was driving at perhaps 40 kilometres per hour and the vehicle by inertia passed through the -- passed under the flyover and stopped. But I still heard sound of shooting behind me, and I could hear bullets hitting the car. At this time I was much younger and very strong. I was physically strong and I weighed perhaps about 120 kilos. I tried to ignite again. I happened to be a professional driver. I tried to reignite the car and move it from there. I thought that someone would come running to my aid if I managed to get away from there. So with my left foot and my left arm, I managed to reignite the vehicle. I pressed the clutch and headed off to the Prijedor post office, the main post office in Prijedor. You go straight down a street from the flyover straight to the centre. After a while, I got lost. I was bleeding profusely. There were bloodstains on my white overcoat. My right arm -- I couldn't feel my right arm, and the same goes for my right leg. I didn't notice anything in particular, but I felt a very strong searing pain and I could see bloodstains. Again I tried to move the vehicle. I moved a further 100 metres down the road but then the car stopped. The car stopped dead in its tracks and wouldn't reignite. So there I remained alone in the car just lying, sprawling over the seat. After quite some time, someone came and found me there, a young man. He took me to the hospital, but he took the long way to the hospital because, as he later told me, I kept falling unconscious and then coming to. I was taken to the hospital. This young man took me to the hospital. I was administered first aid, and they sent me off to Banja Luka, and then the same day from Banja Luka to Belgrade by plane. I was seriously injured, very seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your speed as you were reaching the flyover?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was in the town itself, so my speed was about 40 kilometres per hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you recognised some of the assailants. Did you notice whether they in turn recognised you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I got a clear look, and I recognised them clearly. Among the assailants there were three persons whom I knew rather well. Among Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 11219 to 11227. those three there was one person whom I knew particularly well, and this person knew me particularly well for the simple reason that I had in the past bought him so many drinks that it would have been impossible for him not to recognise me. He is a native of Prijedor and so am I.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far from the vehicle were the people who were shooting at you under the flyover standing and were they shooting as you were approaching or after you had driven past them already?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: They fired on me when I had just barely driven past them, and you can tell from my injuries, from the kind of injuries that I suffered, you can tell that they were shooting from close range and sort of from the side. So after I'd just driven past them with the front part of my car, as I was still passing, they opened fire on me and on the front seat of my vehicle. They were standing to my right, maybe a metre and a half, up to 2 metres. On the left side they were perhaps the width of a lane far from my car and they were standing on the pavement behind the pillars of the flyover itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you reached the flyover, you said you'd seen people running across the road. Which side were they coming from? Which building were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I saw them as I was already beginning to drive into the passage, into the pass under the flyover. They were crossing from left to right. On the left-hand side of the road there is a flight of stairs taking you from the bus terminal and railway station down, and to the right there is another flight of stairs leading up to Puharska and what we refer to as the small overfly. What really happened is that I cut their column across the road in two as they were trying to take up position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that at this moment they had already overpowered the people who were in charge of securing the railway station?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but that must have been the case because that would have been the only way for them to reach the flyover from the railway station. The only way to the flyover for them would have led past the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which direction were the attackers moving in?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I could see, it was from left to right. That's where they were standing. Some of them were on the left-hand side of the road and some on the right. Some of them were crossing. That means that that was their general direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By taking the flyover, which road did the assailants cut off?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's the main road into Prijedor itself, from the direction of Banja Luka and from Bosanska Dubica, from Bosanski Novi, from the army positions, from the hospital, and from Urije, where the police were stationed, the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, by taking this position, the attackers on Prijedor cut the town off virtually from the barracks as well as from the place where the reserve police were stationed.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would very much have been the case. And I'm sure it was their aim to take that particular position in order to prevent aid from reaching the town's defenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You used a sound to explain what the shooting sounded like. That was not reflected in the transcript, however. The sounds of shooting that you heard when you were wounded, was that an automatic weapon being fired?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was automatic fire. But the fire came from a number of different weapons. Judging by my wounds, my injuries, and the photographs that were taken of my injuries, you could see that they used bolt [Realtime transcript read in error "both"] rifles, semi-automatic and automatic weapons, because I had splinters and bullets in me, a very large number of them. I had many bullets in my body and shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could I just ask for clarification. I thought I heard the interpreter say "bolt rifles," but the transcript says "both." I thought it was "b-o-l-t," but I'm not sure if I misheard that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution counsel is right, "bolt action rifles."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as you could see, was there just one person shooting at you or more than one person?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: More than one person shot at me. I saw a number of them in that group. Among them I knew quite a few. And judging by my wounds -- I had 32 penetration wounds altogether, gunshot wounds, and it was obvious that the fire came from a number of different sources, that is, a number of people shot at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about your wounds. Can you please now tell us where exactly were you wounded.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded in the right upper leg. It was cut into and the bone in my upper leg sustained a damage in the length of 7 centimetres. I was also wounded in the right lower arm. The right upper arm with the collarbone, I still have screws in that bone, and the same is true of my right upper leg. I have an iron plate and 18 screws that hold my leg together and enable me to walk. Then I also had a gunshot wound, a penetration wound, in the left upper leg; in the left lower arm, another penetration wound there. In my chest, also a penetration wound. In the stomach, again another penetration wound. In the neck, another penetration wound there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear later on how many people were killed or injured by the attackers on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. While I was hospitalised in Belgrade and later on when I returned, I heard that on that same day 18 young men were killed and that about 36 people, including myself, were slightly or seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like the usher now to show the witness an exhibit marked by the Prosecution, 65 ter number 452. Sorry, it's the Defence 65 ter number 452, but we got the document from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Provisionally marked as D53.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, in front of you you can see a list of people. Can you please read the title of that list.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: "Aggressors on Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among these names, do you recognise any of the people whom you recognised on that morning as your assailants, those people who attacked you and the ambulance which you were driving? And if you could please give us the number first and then the name.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Number 11, Nedzad Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you also tell us how you know that person and for how long.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew him for a long time. That young man grew up in Prijedor, just as I did. We grew up together. And he together with another man was the leader of that group under the flyover. Number 17, Sead Halvadzic, he was also in that group. Benjamin Jukic. I apologise. Number 77, Benjamin Jukic. Number 100, Edo Cajic, Edin. He was a snooker pool maker, and that's how he was known. He was the second in command of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 93 --

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Number 93, Agan Sikiric. He was a teacher. I know him well. And he was also in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no family name Sikiric in this list.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That is true, but I know very well that his nickname is Agan and that he was a teacher in Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you also know other people in this list, at least some of them, but you cannot identify them as the persons who attacked you on that morning?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That is true. I'm sure I know them. When I looked at the list, I saw a name under 73, Kadiric from Rizvanovici, also known as Politicki. He was my colleague. We worked together in the hospital. He was also an ambulance driver. I know that already in the year 1990 on the eve of the elections he was always making jokes and he always promised that one day he would become a politician. That's why he got his nickname, Politicki, which means "politician."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We will not need this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is my understanding that you tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear objections, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, there are -- my comments would go to the weight of this document. Counsel hasn't indicated, but it's my understanding it was seized by the OTP from the Prijedor police station, and that's the only source of how it was compiled or who compiled it or what the sources of information of the names are. But I think that goes to the weight given the Court's previous rulings about the weight and authenticity not affecting initial admission we submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Due to -- and following the practice and what was submitted to the parties before starting the case, it has nothing to do with the evaluation of evidence and it serves, no doubt, for a better understanding of the witness before us. Admitted into evidence as D53A and B respectfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, after you were wounded, did you have to undergo the assessment of your ability to work? Were you then proclaimed to be handicapped and what is the degree of your handicap?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was retired as unable to continue working. I have been found as being 90 per cent disabled by a medical board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we announced your arrival as a Defence witness - that was a few weeks ago - you were not able to come at that time. Why were you not able to come?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The main reason is the fact that I suffered a heart -- a minor heart episode at that time, and immediately after that I got pneumonia because of all the surgical procedures that I had to undergo, and there were 16 of them altogether. And because of the transplantation, that is, the blood that I had to be given during each surgery, my immunity is now impaired so that I am now very prone to all sorts of infections and my heart doesn't work as well as it used to work before all these surgeries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the time before you were wounded but after the takeover in Prijedor. After the takeover, did your colleagues continue coming to work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Many colleagues stopped showing up for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did somebody fire them or they just simply failed to show up for work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Some of my colleagues stopped coming to work back in 1991. And the main reason why I had to return from Slavonija was the fact that the hospital sent a request, either a written or an oral request to the army to send me back home, because there were other drivers who no longer wanted to work. That's why I was demobilised in October or in November 1991. I don't remember exactly when it was, but in any case, I stayed in Slavonija for a very brief period of time. In 1992, some colleagues left work. Among them there were also some Serbs who no longer wanted to work. Mostly those were the people who had sent their families away from Prijedor or simply moved their families out of Prijedor before the breakout of any conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those colleagues of yours who did not want to work as ambulance drivers and as a result of that you were demobilised, do you know their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims. And if you want me to tell you, I can give you their names. Kadiric, Blazevic, Delkic, Crnalic. Those are the guys who had worked with me for a number of years before that and all of a sudden they stopped coming to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that there were also Serbs who stopped showing up for work. Can you give us any of their names?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Among them was my colleague and neighbour who was not a driver but who worked with me in the hospital. His name is Vid Djakovic. He also left work. He -- Vinko Latinovic also left work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those who continued coming to work after the takeover in Prijedor, did they continue to work normally as every day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, we worked in shifts, but there was no public transportation at the time. It didn't function normally. And also, there were checkpoints manned by people in various settlements and neighbourhoods, and there were a number of people who had to work in 48-hour shifts. And then the director or our superior ordered us to take these people home, but even we could not drive all over the place. We would take them as close as possible to their homes and then they would continue on foot. Those who lived closer to the hospital had to bear the brunt of that -- the requirements of work at that time because they could go home, change, take a little rest, and come back to continue working at the hospital. It was easier for them than for those who lived far away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are saying that the circumstances were very special and that as a result of that some people had to work for 48 hours without any breaks. The hospital management faced the same problems. Do you know whether a crisis staff was set up at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the end of that month, the month of May, I heard that a crisis staff had been established in the hospital. Its main task was to facilitate the functioning of all the services in the hospital, starting with the technical services, medical services, and so on and so forth, because of the events that preceded the setting up of checkpoints and roadblocks and due to the fact that people were not able to come to work or leave work, but I cannot remember who the members of that crisis staff were. They were employees of the hospital, but I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have said that the crisis staff in the hospital was established in late May. Does that mean a few days before you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly how it happened. It may have been on the 24th or on the 25th. I can't recall the date, but I know that the crisis staff was established and that its task was to facilitate the work of all the services in the hospital. I know that they even changed the shift of the guards, because there was a shortage of people at the time. So in order to make everybody's life easier, they had to rearrange the shifts of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that crisis staffs were also set up in other companies?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were stories about crisis staffs being established in order to facilitate the work of the companies, various companies, in terms of the functioning of their various services and departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you return from Belgrade after your hospital treatment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I returned 18 months later from the hospital treatment in Belgrade. During that period of time, I was at various rehabilitation centres and at the military medical academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that from the moment you were wounded, you were absent from Prijedor for 18 months?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I was away for 18 months after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the war ended in Prijedor, did you ever meet a person named Dragan, Tomas? Where did you meet this person and how did you get to know this person?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tomas Dragan.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met this gentleman last year, and I happened to know him quite well because he worked at the graveyard and we used to call him "undertaker." I was a jestful nickname that we used. Last year I think at the beginning last year -- of the last year - I can't remember the month - he came to Prijedor and he would go to cafes that I usually go to, the same cafes, as well as other people in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another thing I'd like to ask you is whether you know Dr. Stakic, what was the first time you heard of him.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I know Dr. Stakic. I've known him since before 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you known him personally since before 1990 or had you just heard of him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not personally. I'd merely heard of him through my colleagues at work, as those were the doctors who signed our orders for -- as ambulance drivers, transport orders. And I heard that there was a Dr. Stakic working in Omarska at the health centre. That was prior to 1990. As I reside in Prijedor, in the 1990s I heard of him when the elections took place. After that I heard that he had become the vice-president of the municipal assembly in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any rumours surrounding Dr. Stakic's appointment as the vice-president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with this. The rumour was out that a small man - and I don't mean to offend anyone - from a small village could become the vice-president of the municipal assembly. And we, the natives of Prijedor, were left out. So everyone was asking themselves, how come none of the native candidates were appointed as the vice-president. But I also heard something else at that time: Word was that Dr. Stakic, who was a doctor, had been appointed vice-president through political channels. They said that the coalition that was in power at that time, the coalition between the SDS and his party, had granted him the place of vice-president. His party was not a party that was based in Prijedor; it was based in Omarska. The party was called Radical something. I cannot really remember. But it was not the same radical party that was in Prijedor. I'm talk about Mr. Seselj's radical party, and there were some other people there. Dr. Stakic was a member of a different radical party. And I know about the SDS because I was at this time a member of the SDS. I didn't take part in any of the meetings or anything. Everyone knew what the elections were for. They were aimed at -- to bring about the downfall of the one-party system so that everyone could make up their own minds as to which party they would vote. So my idea was that I should opt for the SDS. I was familiar with their platform and they were my choice. So the story was that the SDS had given them, granted them the position of the vice-president, although the SDS was, according to the election results, entitled to fill that particular position. I also know that during this same period many people in Prijedor were angry. They were infuriated that someone like him, from a small village, a man no one really knew, was appointed to an important position in the municipal assembly. Myself, I don't think it was much of a position, you know, in terms of decision-making. But that's what people in Prijedor were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The other people in power, the other people occupying important positions, were all of them from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: 90 or more per cent of those people were natives of Prijedor. The president of the municipal assembly was Mr. Cehajic, Mrs. Cehajic's husband. His wife is a doctor. As far as I remember, the president of the executive board, the late Dr. Mico, also a native of Prijedor. And those other officials were also from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you meet Dr. Stakic in person?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I met him in person when I went to the occupational medicine unit to see Dr. Savic, because she was prescribing my therapy and the painkillers they still use, as well as a number of other medications. That was when I met Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the transcript - because it is not reflected in the transcript - did you say "when I returned from Belgrade from the military medical academy"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which month, in which year you came back from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the month, but the year was 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sometimes see Dr. Stakic in cafes, and who else came there? Who was he normally with? Who was keeping him company, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I sometimes saw Dr. Stakic in a cafe, in a coffee house called Kod Pale and also in another cafe called Top, where people shoot pool. I used to go there a lot myself. There weren't many cafes around that were open. Of course people came there, and I could see him too. I'd also see the late Dr. Mico. I saw him quite many times. But he was never shooting pool. He'd just stand there, like myself, and he liked to tease people, those who were shooting pool. Dr. Stakic was among them. A number of people told me that he was a very good player. At the same cafe I saw other people from Prijedor. I saw a number of other people too there, so I'm not sure who you refer to. Did you mean anyone specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to specify. When you were spending time in those places, did you ever see Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Simo would come in with a retinue. They were a group that he socialised with. They would have a drink, and those people he came with were actually his official escort. But he was - how should I put it? - you know, he'd just drop by to have a drink and then he would leave. He never joined the others who were shooting pool.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Simo Drljaca in those cafes socialising with Dr. Stakic, regardless of whether they were shooting pool together or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
