utterances.text: No. I'm talking about what I saw. They didn't socialise, no. I even heard rumours that they were not on the best of terms and that that dated back to a long time ago. I'm not sure how to put this. Maybe what I told you before when I was speaking about a small man being appointed vice-president of the assembly and not even being from Prijedor, maybe that was the source of tension between the two of them, but I know that they were not on very friendly terms. Simo had his own people that he'd usually spend time with, people who surrounded him, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dragojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my examination. Now there'll be questions from the Prosecution and from the Honourable Chamber. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's appropriate to have the break now. The trial stands adjourned until ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Dragojevic, thank you for answering this line of questions which no doubt were extremely difficult to answer for you, reopening wounds. We are aware they were problematic, and please tell us if you feel uncomfortable and believe that it would be necessary to have an additional break. We would fully understand this. But could you please be so kind and answer now the questions put to you by the Office of the Prosecutor in the same way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, would I be correct in understanding from your testimony that based upon your experience as an ambulance driver for many years, had you not received medical care when you did, those wounds would likely have led to your death?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Had I not been given medical assistance in a timely fashion and had I been taken to a smaller hospital with not as many facilities as the Prijedor hospital, I'm certain I would have succumbed to my wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in 1992 - let's go to before the takeover - how many ambulance drivers were there in Prijedor municipality to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Prior to 1990 -- and I know how many there were at the hospital. And there was another service, duty service at the health centre but also at the hospital. And even in Ljubija you had ambulance drivers, and they would take people from the medical centre in Ljubija to Prijedor. And then if anyone needed to be taken to Zagreb, Ljubljana, or another medical centre from Prijedor, we would take over. In Kozarac there were a number of ambulance drivers too. The shifts were 12, 24, and 48, about 12 drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned Ljubija. Do you recall the names of any of the drivers from Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember Vinko. I remember another man, just that I can't really remember his name now. I do remember Vinko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was this other man a Muslim, the other driver from Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had four drivers -- four, perhaps more, but four working the shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If you recall that name later, perhaps I could get it from you. Sir, I want to go back to the 30th of April, 1992, the day of the takeover of Prijedor. Where were you that evening? Did you participate in any of the activities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was at home this evening. I remember clearly. I worked the day shift until 7.00 in the evening, and after that I went home. I had coffee with another colleague who worked the same shift as I did, a paramedic, Irfan Kurtovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When was it that you learned that Prijedor had been taken over on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I learned the next day, the next morning. When I got up and went to the hospital, that's when I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I imagine - would I be correct? - that on that day you listened to the radio to get the updates as to what was happening. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't say anything specific, and I can't say. But I wasn't listening to the radio. As far as the media are concerned, I like watching football games and I read the sports daily. That's all I used the media for. When I was younger, I was into sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: And that's all that's really left with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So how was it that you learned about the takeover? Was that from colleagues only that you learned information about the takeover?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at the hospital -- my house is some 100 metres or so from the hospital, and I was at the hospital quite often at the time and I worked two or three days in a row. I would only go home to change, take a shower, have a bite to eat, and I would go back to the hospital. So I didn't do 12, 24, 48 hours shifts, like others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, my question is: How did you learn -- who told you about the takeover and -- let me first ask that question. Who told you about the takeover?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: My colleagues, paramedics, and other staff who were at the hospital, we were having our morning cup of coffee and they told me that on that day Prijedor had been taken over. So I didn't learn it from my fellow drivers but other colleagues in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And who were you told had taken over Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have already answered that question, I believe. My colleague, paramedics told me that, and then the guards in the hospital were talking about that. That's how I learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, my question is: Who did they tell you had taken over power? Prijedor was taken over by who? By the Croatian army? Who took over Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: They told me that it was the SDS who had taken over the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: As an SDS member, had you been -- received any weapons prior to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I never carried arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You talked about the fact that you knew Dr. Stakic because you were an ambulance driver and he was a medical doctor. Was it common in Prijedor for people in the medical field to know each other? Was the community small enough that people knew each other?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was normal. Prijedor is a smallish town, and people know each other. That's how I recognise all those people who shot at me. I knew them because I lived in -- I had lived in that town for 33 years when that happened. I was 33 years at that time. And through work I had an opportunity to meet all the doctors. Maybe not all of those who worked in outpatient's surgeries in villages, but those who worked in the health centre, in the occupational medicine, in the hospital, I knew them. It was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you agree based upon what you observed that medical doctors knew each other and that it was likely that other doctors in Prijedor knew Dr. Stakic and vice versa, he knew other medical doctors working in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Whether he knew them personally is up to him to answer whether he had contacts with them. But as far as I know, it was not his duty to have contacts with them. Whether he did or not, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But you just told us that it was common - am I correct - for people to know each other in the medical field and that you, an ambulance driver from Prijedor, knew Dr. Stakic, a doctor from Omarska. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It is true that I heard of Dr. Stakic as a doctor who worked in Omarska. I met him only when I returned from Belgrade. That is when I first saw him like I am looking at you now. That's when I first met him. I knew of him before, just like I heard of the famous Dr. Kurjak who worked in Zagreb but I never met Dr. Kurjak personally. That's what I'm saying. I only met Dr. Stakic when I returned from Belgrade from the medical military academy. Let me tell you another thing: This doesn't imply that Dr. Stakic knew all the doctors in the hospital. Only if he had personal contacts with them did he actually get to meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you as an ambulance driver -- let me withdraw the question. I'm going to move on to another topic. Sir, you indicated that you were -- you went to Kozarac after the attack on Kozarac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I've already told you that I went to Susici during the conflict in Kozarac. Whether that was an attack, I don't know. There's no way for me to know. I was not in Kozarac. I told you that on that day I went as far as Susici. That is where I stopped the car, and there was another driver with me, Mladen Bogdanovic, and he also drove an ambulance on that day. And I was in Kozarac before that, before the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the day that you went following what you call "the conflict," you passed through Kozarusa. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, I went as far as Susici from Prijedor. I can tell you exactly where Susici is. On the left and on the right, there were small shelters of the bus stops and this is where people could wait for the bus. Before that, there is a bridge. As soon as I crossed the bridge, I pulled over at the bus stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but did you pass through Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Everything that is before Kozarac, I had to go through it. All the way up to Susici, where I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you did pass through Kozarusa. Some of us are not as familiar with the area as you are, sir.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And on that day, you transported individuals, some elderly, I believe you said, and some women, to the town of Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I transported people from there to the hospital. There were people who also went on foot, and they were exhausted from walking. It was very hot. So I took them in the ambulance -- I took them to the hospital to be seen by the doctors. Those who didn't want to go to the hospital, I took them to their relatives downtown, to their friends. Some of them I took and left in front of the sports hall. And Mr. Kapetanovic, I took him personally to his brother's -- to his wife's brother's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the people that were left at the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us to the best of your recollection what day this was? And to help you out, I'll remind you that the 24th of May was a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date or day, but I can tell you that it was either the 24th or the 25th. It was then -- you have to understand that after all I have been through, some dates escape me. But I can give you a rough estimate of the time when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's certainly understandable. Was it then after -- sir, did you see or hear about the shelling of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I heard later on. I heard shots and gunfire. But whether it was Kozarac that was shelled, I don't know, because after that I didn't go to Kozarac and soon after that I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you went to -- was it -- I may mispronounce it -- Susici?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Susici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Susici. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you went to Susici and passed through Kozarusa, did you see the effect of shelling or of burning of houses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: By the road I didn't see anything to that effect. And when we reached Susici, the army stopped us because it wasn't safe to go any further. And that is where we took the people that we were supposed to transport either to Prijedor or to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This day that you went to Susici, was this at the end of a 48-hour shift? Was it the second day of your shift? Was it the beginning of your shift? Can you tell us if you were working the day before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Before these conflicts, I've already told you there were very few drivers in the hospital, and that's why I was demobilised and I returned from Slavonija. I worked practically all the time in the hospital with two other colleagues of mine who even slept there, and I went home from time to time to either have a bath or have a bite to eat, and then half an hour later I would return to the hospital to continue working. My house was very close. That's why I could go home. But having said that, I can also tell you that I was present at the hospital practically all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. So, sir, having been present at the hospital almost all the time, would it be correct that what you've told us about the people you transported from the Kozarac area - I know you said it was from Susici - that those were -- and you've told us about all the people that you transported from that area over those few days of the 24th, 25th, 26th of May, 1992. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question. What was the question, whether it was correct that I transported these people? Yes, I did transport them to the hospital to Pecani, and some I left in front of the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. The persons that you transported, were they wounded?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. They were -- may I? May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were elderly people who had walked from Kozarac to Susici. There were also women carrying children, and those were the people who could not walk any further, who said they needed medical attention, and our superiors had given us the task to transport all such people to the hospital for medical check-ups or to their relatives, if they expressed the wish to go to their relatives rather than to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. During the previous day, did you ever transport any wounded persons from the Brdo region, from Hambarine or surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the previous days I did not transport any wounded, either from Brdo or wherever you say. On the previous days I took a pregnant lady to Kozarac. I was accompanied by a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just stopping you because you've answered my question, and you've already told us about transporting the pregnant woman. Sir, I understand that you told us that you viewed your job as to help anyone who was injured, regardless of their ethnicity. If you had received permission -- let me first ask you: Do you know a Dr. Idriz Merdzanic who was from Prijedor but was working in Kozarac when the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know the doctor personally, but I heard that there were doctors, many doctors up there, but I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you become aware that Dr. Merdzanic asked Colonel Zeljaja to allow the evacuation of two dying children from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you had been made aware of that, you would have taken those children to the hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: If they had been down there in Susici, of course I would have taken all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that after -- excuse me. Sir, you said that after Dr. Stakic was named the vice-president of the municipality, people said some insulting things about that appointment and used words to the effect of "a small man from a small village was in such an important position." Would it be correct that you felt that those were insulting words?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were insulting. However, at that time, as far as these people are concerned, they had the right to express their opinion because they felt sorry that somebody from a village made it to the municipality, and there were people in the town, and it was well known at the time why Dr. Stakic came and that was because the SDS gave his party a position in the municipal assembly. That was the story that could be heard in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this man who was described as a small man from a small village rose to become the president of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor not once but two times; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know because I don't know what happened once I had to go to the VMA. When I left, he was the vice-president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one minor question related to your testimony on page 24, line 15 and following -- it's only for informing the parties what I'm discussing you. You need not take care that we are referring to our transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At that previous -- during your examination-in-chief you mentioned that once you went to the Crisis Staff in Cirkin Polje. "There was a house there, and as far as I can remember - it was a long time ago, mind you - there was Mr. Kuruzovic there and his staff were in charge of issuing certificates." Can you please tell us - you mentioned it was in the month of May - was this a permanent institution, a permanent building where the Crisis Staff resided in Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That building is close to where I live. It was just an ordinary house that was adapted and turned into a storage or a warehouse. In the front of the building, there was an office and visitors and clients would go into that office. We did the same whenever we went there to fetch the certificates for petrol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I still don't have any kind of image of this building. Can you tell us the size of this building, how many floors, how many rooms approximately?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It had a ground floor and a first floor. How many rooms it had, I don't know. I only went there on official business, and I would only enter the front room. I would get the certificate. I would sign the receipt, and with that certificate I could get petrol. At that time there was a shortage of fuel, and I believe that it was their task to supervise the rational use of petrol. I was not the only one who went there as an ambulance driver. I also saw the drivers who worked for the fire brigade and also civilians who needed petrol to maybe go to Banja Luka or some business or elsewhere. So there were other people besides me who went to that house. It is just an ordinary family house. I even know the owner of that house. His last name is Sabljic. It used to be his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At that time was the house specially marked, that everybody knew this was a building of the Crisis Staff? Were there special emblems or insignia at the building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice any marks, but since I know the area -- I lived there in the vicinity -- I was told that the Crisis Staff was up there and that I could go there to get the certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection - I know it's more than ten years now - who told you? In concreto, who was the person telling you this was the building of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: My boss. The person who was in charge of all the ambulance vehicles, he told me to go to Cirkin Polje. And let me tell you. This is Mr. Sabljic's house, and the company was Merkator based in Slovenia and this is where they bought mushrooms grown -- from growers. And that's how the company -- it was known as the house where this company had its premises and also that was the house where the Crisis Staff issued petrol certificates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that it was limited to issue petrol certificates; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The only purpose of my going there were petrol certificates. That's where we could obtain them. And that was the sole purpose of my visits to that house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to repeat the question. I fully understood that for you it was the sole purpose, but were there also other people requesting other certificates on other issues issued by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, because my question was not that clear: Could one read at the entrance door or somewhere else on the building the words "Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think at the main door, the main entrance, there was a cardboard sign, if I remember correctly, which said "Crisis Staff." As soon as you approached the door, someone would be there to ask you who you were there to see or what it was that you needed. And I told the person immediately that I needed the certificate, so it only took them a short while to get one for me. And then I went straight off to the petrol station to get petrol. Both myself and the other two colleagues who worked with me, they would also go there to fetch their certificates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And on the certificate as such, one could read that it was issued by the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, when was it that the first time you went to this building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the first time was around the 23rd or thereabouts. And after that I went twice or three times perhaps because we were taking patients from the hospital to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it's reflected correctly on the transcript, 23rd would be 23rd of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have no additional questions myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I hope I have only one question for you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You remember you told us about a young man being killed who was a Serb and you told us also that you knew the killer who was the son of some Muslim. That was on page 24, line 10 for the parties. This killer, was ever brought to court? Was prosecuted, indicted, or something?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Whether ever an indictment was issued against him, I don't know. These are legal matters. I know nothing about that. But as far as I know, he was never even brought in to the police station, the SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And were there other incidents similar to this, that not need to be a killing but persons threatened or something like that and the perpetrators were never brought into the police station or something?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really not familiar with that. I was not familiar with that, with those particular documents or whatever I should call them, but I know that many such people were never even brought in. The people who attacked me were never brought in either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only one. And I forgot -- Honourable Judge Argibay reminded me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever seen any of the perpetrators who attempted to murder you in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Several months ago or perhaps one or two months ago I saw one of them in the centre. He was one of the perpetrators in the attack against me. He was one of the people who were shooting at me. And he was walking about freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It remains for me to thank you on behalf of the entire Trial Chamber and the parties for coming to The Hague to give us your testimony, which no doubt was extremely difficult for you, recalling that what happened to you and apparently has still an impact on your daily life. And it is for us to assist and to do what we can to avoid that some things like this will happen in the future too and that those being responsible for these crimes will be held criminally liable for this and that there is no chance in this our world that there is something like impunity and persons are not taken responsible for that what happened, for instance, against you. So once again, thank you very much, and we all wish you a safe trip home to your home country. You are excused for today. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First I have not yet get a final confirmation whether we can switch to the morning session on Wednesday, but in all likelihood it will -- the session on Wednesday will take place in the morning instead of the afternoon. I'll inform you as soon as possible tomorrow morning when the other Trial Chamber has conferred. From Friday's session, it remains open that there were provided on a request of the Chamber three stills of Exhibit S157. I think both parties had the possibility to have a look on these documents. If there are no objections, these documents would be admitted into evidence as S157-2, -3, and -4. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: They are admitted into evidence under these numbers. Anything else to be discussed? Not that I can see. This concludes today's session. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
